igcse-0580-bounds-single-measurements.description: Core and Extended. Find lower and upper bounds by halving the spacing between rounded readings.

sections.title: How low could the reading have been?
sections.label: Start
sections.intro: First imagine the previous reading on a number line. The point halfway between it and the given reading is the lower cut-off.

blocks.html: Move down by half one rounding step to find the lower bound.

figure.alt: Number line from 38 to 40, with half steps at 38.5 and 39.5.
figure.caption: The two midpoints mark the edges of the band.

blocks.prompt: A roll of fabric measures 47 m to the nearest metre. Give the lower bound in metres.
blocks.hint: Find the midpoint between the given reading and its neighbour.
blocks.solution:
The spacing between readings is 1 m. Half that spacing is 0.5 m.

Start at the recorded length and move down by 0.5 m: \(47-0.5\).

The answer is \(46.5\).

retry.feedback: The cut-off is halfway to the next reading, not a full metre away.

blocks.html: Use half the spacing between readings. A full step lands on a different rounded value.

blocks.prompt: A roll of fabric measures 56 m to the nearest metre. Give the lower bound in metres.
blocks.hint: Find the midpoint between the given reading and its neighbour.
blocks.solution:
The spacing between readings is 1 m. Half that spacing is 0.5 m.

Start at the recorded length and move down by 0.5 m: \(56-0.5\).

The answer is \(55.5\).

retry.feedback: The cut-off is halfway to the next reading, not a full metre away.

sections.title: Where does the next reading begin?
sections.label: End
sections.intro: The midpoint above the recorded value is where the next rounding band begins. The measurement can approach this cutoff from below.

blocks.html: The upper bound is halfway from the given reading to the next reading.

blocks.prompt: A roll of fabric measures 50 m to the nearest metre. Give the upper bound in metres.
blocks.hint: Find the midpoint between the given reading and its neighbour.
blocks.solution:
The spacing between readings is 1 m. Half that spacing is 0.5 m.

Start at the recorded length and move up by 0.5 m: \(50+0.5\).

The answer is \(50.5\).

retry.feedback: The cut-off is halfway to the next reading, not a full metre away.

blocks.html: Keep the exact cut-off. There is no need to write a string of 9s just below it.

blocks.prompt: A roll of fabric measures 59 m to the nearest metre. Give the upper bound in metres.
blocks.hint: Find the midpoint between the given reading and its neighbour.
blocks.solution:
The spacing between readings is 1 m. Half that spacing is 0.5 m.

Start at the recorded length and move up by 0.5 m: \(59+0.5\).

The answer is \(59.5\).

retry.feedback: The cut-off is halfway to the next reading, not a full metre away.

sections.title: What changes with decimal places?
sections.label: Scale
sections.intro: Find the last place recorded on the scale. A measurement to two decimal places has one hundredth between possible readings.

blocks.html: To 2 decimal places the step is 0.01, so halve it to get 0.005.

blocks.prompt: A scale shows 3.26 kg, rounded to 2 decimal places. Give the lower bound in kilograms.
blocks.hint: Two decimal places gives a step of one hundredth, not one tenth.
blocks.solution:
Two decimal places means the spacing is 0.01 kg.

Half the spacing is 0.005 kg.

Subtract from the reading: \(3.26-0.005\).

The answer is \(3.255\).

retry.feedback: This subtracts half a tenth. Here the last recorded place is hundredths.

blocks.html: For two decimal places, subtracting 0.05 uses the wrong scale.

blocks.prompt: A scale shows 3.47 kg, rounded to 2 decimal places. Give the lower bound in kilograms.
blocks.hint: Two decimal places gives a step of one hundredth, not one tenth.
blocks.solution:
Two decimal places means the spacing is 0.01 kg.

Half the spacing is 0.005 kg.

Subtract from the reading: \(3.47-0.005\).

The answer is \(3.465\).

retry.feedback: This subtracts half a tenth. Here the last recorded place is hundredths.

igcse-0580-bounds-error-intervals.description: Core and Extended. Write a complete error interval and explain its open and closed ends.

sections.title: How do I show both cut-offs together?
sections.label: Nearest
sections.intro: Once you have the two bounds, write the unknown quantity between them. The exact value may be anywhere inside that region.

blocks.html: Write \(L\le x<U\) when a positive value is rounded to a fixed step. The inequality includes the lower bound.

figure.alt: Number line with a filled dot at 215 and an open dot at 225.
figure.caption: The filled dot includes \(215\). The open dot excludes \(225\).

blocks.prompt: A measurement of \(x\) m is recorded as 500 m to the nearest 10 m. Give the error interval for \(x\).
blocks.hint: Show the two cut-offs and decide which one belongs in the interval.
blocks.solution:
Two successive readings are 10 m apart, so the half step is 5 m.

Subtract and add 5 to find the two cut-off points.

The lower cut-off rounds to the given reading. The upper cut-off rounds to the next reading.

Write \(495\le x<505\).

retry.feedback: Check the top end. At the upper bound the value rounds to the next reading.

blocks.html: Use a less-than sign at the upper end. Beyond that cut-off, the value rounds to a different reading.

blocks.prompt: A measurement of \(x\) m is recorded as 590 m to the nearest 10 m. Give the error interval for \(x\).
blocks.hint: Show the two cut-offs and decide which one belongs in the interval.
blocks.solution:
Two successive readings are 10 m apart, so the half step is 5 m.

Subtract and add 5 to find the two cut-off points.

The lower cut-off rounds to the given reading. The upper cut-off rounds to the next reading.

Write \(585\le x<595\).

retry.feedback: Check the top end. At the upper bound the value rounds to the next reading.

sections.title: What if the accuracy uses significant figures?
sections.label: Digits
sections.intro: Underline the last significant digit and name its place. For example, 460 g to two significant figures has its last significant digit in the tens column.

blocks.html: Find the neighbouring rounded readings, then take a midpoint on each side. In these examples the neighbours are one ten apart.

blocks.prompt: A mass \(x\) g is recorded as 400 g correct to 2 significant figures. Give the error interval for \(x\).
blocks.hint: Count the significant digits from the first non-zero digit. Find the place of the second digit.
blocks.solution:
The second significant digit in 400 is the tens digit.

The nearest-ten step is 10 g. Subtract and add 5 g from 400 g.

Include the lower end. Exclude the upper end because it rounds up.

Write \(395\le x<405\).

retry.feedback: Check the top end. At the upper bound the value rounds to the next reading.

blocks.html: At a place-value boundary the two neighbours can have different spacings. Look at both neighbours.

blocks.prompt: A mass \(x\) g is recorded as 430 g correct to 2 significant figures. Give the error interval for \(x\).
blocks.hint: Count the significant digits from the first non-zero digit. Find the place of the second digit.
blocks.solution:
The second significant digit in 430 is the tens digit.

The nearest-ten step is 10 g. Subtract and add 5 g from 430 g.

Include the lower end. Exclude the upper end because it rounds up.

Write \(425\le x<435\).

retry.feedback: Check the top end. At the upper bound the value rounds to the next reading.

sections.title: Which dot should be filled?
sections.label: Endpoints
sections.intro: A filled dot shows an included end. An open dot shows a value that the interval approaches but never reaches.

blocks.html: At a fixed rounding step, the lower midpoint rounds up to the recorded value and the upper midpoint rounds up to the next one.

blocks.prompt: A machine displays a width \(x\) cm as 8.4 cm to the nearest 0.1 cm. Write the error interval for \(x\).
blocks.hint: Use a closed point at the lower end and an open point at the upper end.
blocks.solution:
The cut-offs are halfway to the next readings: \(8.35\) and \(8.45\).

\(8.35\) rounds up to the displayed width. The other cut-off rounds up to the next tenth.

Write \(8.35\le x<8.45\).

retry.feedback: Check the top end. At the upper bound the value rounds to the next reading.

blocks.html: Checking how each midpoint itself rounds is a quick way to choose the inequality signs.

igcse-0580-bounds-sums-products.description: Extended (E1.10). Choose the right ends of measurement intervals for totals, differences and areas.

sections.title: Which ends make a total largest?
sections.label: Total
sections.intro: Length added to length gives a longer total. Make both measurements as large as allowed when finding the upper bound.

blocks.html: For a sum, combine upper with upper, or lower with lower.

blocks.prompt: Two strips measure 41 cm and 21 cm, each to the nearest centimetre. Find the upper bound for their combined length in centimetres.
blocks.hint: Find the longest allowed value at each end of the join.
blocks.solution:
The upper bounds are \(41+0.5=41.5\) and \(21+0.5=21.5\).

Making either strip longer raises the total. Add these two upper bounds.

The answer is \(63\).

retry.feedback: That sum uses the rounded lengths. Start with their upper bounds.

blocks.html: Round only if the question requests it. Keep the exact bounds while combining them.

blocks.prompt: Two strips measure 47 cm and 24 cm, each to the nearest centimetre. Find the upper bound for their combined length in centimetres.
blocks.hint: Find the longest allowed value at each end of the join.
blocks.solution:
The upper bounds are \(47+0.5=47.5\) and \(24+0.5=24.5\).

Making either strip longer raises the total. Add these two upper bounds.

The answer is \(72\).

retry.feedback: That sum uses the rounded lengths. Start with their upper bounds.

sections.title: Which ends make a gap smallest?
sections.label: Gap
sections.intro: If the opening shrinks, the gap shrinks. If the object inside grows, the gap also shrinks. These changes point to opposite ends of the intervals.

blocks.html: For the lower bound of a difference, subtract the upper bound of the second measurement from the lower bound of the first.

figure.alt: A case leaves a narrow gap inside the opening.
figure.caption: A longer case or a shorter opening makes the gap smaller.

blocks.prompt: A shelf opening measures 47 cm and a case measures 20 cm, both to the nearest centimetre. Find the lower bound for the unused width in centimetres.

field.label: Lower bound of the gap in cm

blocks.hint: A smaller opening and a larger case leave a smaller gap.
blocks.solution:
The smallest opening is 46.5 cm. The case can approach 20.5 cm.

Use the smallest opening and the upper cut-off for the case: \(46.5-20.5\).

The answer is \(26\).

retry.feedback: Subtracting both lower bounds keeps the rounded gap. Use the opposite ends.

blocks.html: Subtracting lower from lower does not give the smallest possible gap.

blocks.prompt: A shelf opening measures 53 cm and a case measures 23 cm, both to the nearest centimetre. Find the lower bound for the unused width in centimetres.

field.label: Lower bound of the gap in cm

blocks.hint: A smaller opening and a larger case leave a smaller gap.
blocks.solution:
The smallest opening is 52.5 cm. The case can approach 23.5 cm.

Use the smallest opening and the upper cut-off for the case: \(52.5-23.5\).

The answer is \(29\).

retry.feedback: Subtracting both lower bounds keeps the rounded gap. Use the opposite ends.

sections.title: Which rectangle has the least area?
sections.label: Area
sections.intro: With positive sides, making either side shorter makes the area smaller. Find both lower side limits before multiplying.

blocks.html: For the least area, use the two lower bounds. For the upper bound, use the two upper bounds.

figure.alt: A smaller rectangle shares one corner with a larger rectangle.
figure.caption: Reducing either side reduces the rectangle's area.

blocks.prompt: A rectangular sign measures 29 cm by 10 cm, both to the nearest centimetre. Find the lower bound for the area in square centimetres.
blocks.hint: A smaller positive length and a smaller positive width give a smaller area.
blocks.solution:
The smallest side lengths are \(28.5\) cm and \(9.5\) cm.

Both are positive. Multiply the lower bounds: \(28.5\times9.5\).

The answer is \(270.75\).

retry.feedback: The product of the readings is an estimate of the area, not its lower bound.

blocks.html: Use square units for area. Keep any decimal parts in the lengths.

blocks.hint: A smaller positive length and a smaller positive width give a smaller area.
blocks.solution:

The answer is \(204.75\).

retry.feedback: The product of the readings is an estimate of the area, not its lower bound.

retry.feedback: That sum uses the rounded lengths. Start with their upper bounds.

revision.body:
Which ends make a total largest?

For a sum, combine upper with upper, or lower with lower.

Which ends make a gap smallest?

For the lower bound of a difference, subtract the upper bound of the second measurement from the lower bound of the first.

Which rectangle has the least area?

For the least area, use the two lower bounds. For the upper bound, use the two upper bounds.

igcse-0580-bounds-quotients-decisions.description: Extended (E1.10). Use the bounds of distance and time to find a speed limit, then apply bounds to a fit decision.

sections.title: How can a journey be as slow as possible?
sections.label: Slow
sections.intro: For the slowest journey, pick a distance near the smallest allowed value and a time near the largest. The denominator works in the opposite direction to the numerator.

blocks.html: For positive quantities, the lower bound of a quotient is the lower numerator divided by the upper denominator.

figure.alt: The distance and time bars show the short distance and long time used for a low speed.
figure.caption: Use the lower distance and the upper time to get a lower bound for speed.

blocks.prompt: A robot travels 88 m to the nearest metre in 11 s to the nearest second. Find the lower bound of average speed in metres per second. Give your answer exactly.
blocks.hint: For the lower speed, use a shorter journey in more time.
blocks.solution:
The speed is distance divided by time. Use distance \(87.5\) m and time \(11.5\) s.

Divide \(\frac{87.5}{11.5}\), then give the exact result.

The answer is \(\frac{175}{23}\).

retry.feedback: This uses the displayed readings. Choose the appropriate bounds first.

blocks.html: Using two lower limits can make the answer too high because it also makes the time too short.

blocks.prompt: A robot travels 103 m to the nearest metre in 14 s to the nearest second. Find the lower bound of average speed in metres per second. Give your answer exactly.
blocks.hint: For the lower speed, use a shorter journey in more time.
blocks.solution:
The speed is distance divided by time. Use distance \(102.5\) m and time \(14.5\) s.

Divide \(\frac{102.5}{14.5}\), then give the exact result.

The answer is \(\frac{205}{29}\).

retry.feedback: This uses the displayed readings. Choose the appropriate bounds first.

sections.title: How can a journey be as fast as possible?
sections.label: Fast
sections.intro: For the highest speed, combine a long distance with a short time. Check both pieces of rounding information before dividing.

blocks.html: Find the upper numerator and the lower denominator. The lower denominator must be positive.

blocks.prompt: A robot travels 93 m to the nearest metre in 12 s to the nearest second. Find the upper bound of average speed in metres per second. Give your answer exactly.
blocks.hint: For the upper speed, use a longer journey in less time.
blocks.solution:
The speed is distance divided by time. Use distance \(93.5\) m and time \(11.5\) s.

Divide \(\frac{93.5}{11.5}\), then give the exact result.

The answer is \(\frac{187}{23}\).

retry.feedback: This uses the displayed readings. Choose the appropriate bounds first.

blocks.html: A bound can be approached without being attained. Write the upper bound as the limiting value.

blocks.prompt: A robot travels 108 m to the nearest metre in 9 s to the nearest second. Find the upper bound of average speed in metres per second. Give your answer exactly.
blocks.hint: For the upper speed, use a longer journey in less time.
blocks.solution:
The speed is distance divided by time. Use distance \(108.5\) m and time \(8.5\) s.

Divide \(\frac{108.5}{8.5}\), then give the exact result.

The answer is \(\frac{217}{17}\).

retry.feedback: This uses the displayed readings. Choose the appropriate bounds first.

sections.title: Can I promise that it will fit?
sections.label: Fit
sections.intro: Test the situation that puts the most demand on the space. A rounded total below the space limit alone cannot justify a guarantee.

blocks.html: Compare the upper bound of the total with the exact capacity. If the total is always below or equal to the capacity, it fits.

blocks.prompt: A tray is exactly 60 cm long. Two bars measured to the nearest centimetre are 38 cm and 22 cm long. Are they guaranteed to fit end to end?
blocks.hint: Compare the upper bound of the total length with the exact tray length.
blocks.solution:
The total bar length is less than \(61\) cm, because each bar is below its own upper bound.

Some allowed totals are above 60 cm, so the fit is uncertain.

retry.feedback: Base a guarantee on every allowed total, including those near its upper cut-off.

blocks.html: If some allowed lengths exceed the available space, the fit is uncertain. It may still fit for shorter lengths.

blocks.prompt: A tray is exactly 70 cm long. Two bars measured to the nearest centimetre are 44 cm and 25 cm long. Are they guaranteed to fit end to end?
blocks.hint: Compare the upper bound of the total length with the exact tray length.
blocks.solution:
The total bar length is less than \(70\) cm, because each bar is below its own upper bound.

The total is always less than 70 cm, so both bars fit.

retry.feedback: Base a guarantee on every allowed total, including those near its upper cut-off.

examples.title: Find the lower bound of a speed
examples.question: A robot travels 58 m to the nearest metre in 11 s to the nearest second. Find the lower bound of average speed in metres per second. Give your answer exactly.
solution: The speed is distance divided by time. Use distance \(57.5\) m and time \(11.5\) s.
Divide \(\frac{57.5}{11.5}\), then give the exact result.
The answer is \(5\).

examples.title: Make a guaranteed fit decision
examples.question:
A tray is exactly 42 cm long. Two bars measured to the nearest centimetre are 26 cm and 16 cm long. Are they guaranteed to fit end to end?

Give Yes or No and explain your answer.
solution: The total bar length is less than \(43\) cm, because each bar is below its own upper bound.
Some allowed totals are above 42 cm, so the fit is uncertain.

examples.title: Make a guaranteed fit decision
examples.question:
A tray is exactly 52 cm long. Two bars measured to the nearest centimetre are 32 cm and 19 cm long. Are they guaranteed to fit end to end?

Give Yes or No and explain your answer.
solution: The total bar length is less than \(52\) cm, because each bar is below its own upper bound.
The total is always less than 52 cm, so both bars fit.
